text: {"master_id":"ted-greene","work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","usage_notes":[{"chord_quality":"maj7","function_role":"harmonic-family-membership","narrative":"Major 7th chords belong to Greene's 'major Group 1' family. Their formula is 1, 3, 5, 7 derived from the major scale: 'major 7th chords have the following formula: 1, 3, 5, 7... the chord tones of an A Major 7th chord would be the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th tones of the A Major scale.' Chapter 1, p. 9.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 1 p.9"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"maj7","function_role":"scale-pairing-major-or-lydian","narrative":"Group 1 major chords — including maj7 — take either the major scale or the Lydian scale: 'group 1 major chords most commonly take one of two scales, either the MAJOR or the LYDIAN. As to which of the two to use, it is almost always a matter of personal preference... they both sound good in most cases.' Chapter 1, p. 10.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","scale-chord-compatibility"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 1 p.10"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"maj7","function_role":"lydian-scale-color-option","narrative":"When using the Lydian scale over a major Group 1 chord, the #4 (raised fourth) is the sole distinguishing tone from the plain major scale: 'the Lydian's, it is simply a Major scale with a #4th instead of the regular 4th.' This raised fourth provides the 'hippest' color of the two options. Chapter 1, p. 10.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 1 p.10"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"maj7","function_role":"upper-partial-extension-system","narrative":"Major 7th chord formulas extend upward via the upper-partial system: when the formula expands to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 it becomes a ninth chord; to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 an eleventh; to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 a thirteenth. 'The 11th is the same letter name as the 4th, and the 13th tone is the same letter name as the 6th.' Chapter 1, p. 10.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 1 p.10"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"maj7","function_role":"position-based-soloing","narrative":"Over major Group 1 chords, the player should combine major and Lydian scale knowledge within a 5-6 fret fingerboard area: 'you will want to know separate scales for the different chords in the song, but if you know enough positions of each scale, you will be able to stay in one little 5 or 6 fret area and play through the whole song.' Chapter 4, p. 60.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:fingerboard-position-system","position-stay-5-6-frets"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.60"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"maj7","function_role":"fingerboard-visualization-requirement","narrative":"Soloing over major Group 1 chords demands active fingerboard visualization, not rote pattern recall: 'Remember to VISUALIZE the notes on the fingerboard as discussed earlier; at the risk of boring you, let me say it again: THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT! It is one of the best things you can do for yourself.' Chapter 4, p. 67.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:fingerboard-position-system","visualize-fingerboard-primary"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.67"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"maj7","function_role":"jazz-waltz-application","narrative":"The major (and Lydian) scale runs learned over major chords can be applied in 3/4 time: '3/4 time can be very attractive in jazz, creating the feel known as \"Jazz Waltz\". You may find it highly stimulating for variety's sake, to make up some runs in 3/4 time... or even just using the Major (or Lydian) scale.' Chapter 4, p. 71.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:rhythmic-articulation-system"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.71"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"min7","function_role":"harmonic-family-membership","narrative":"The minor 7th chord formula is 1, b3, 5, b7 derived from the major scale: 'Minor 7th chord has the following formula: 1, b3, 5, b7... a C Minor 7th chord would contain the following tones: 1C, b3Eb, 5G and b7Bb, which are the 1st, flatted 3rd, 5th and flatted 7th tones of the C Major scale.' Chapter 1, p. 9.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 1 p.9"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"min7","function_role":"scale-pairing-minor-7th-scale","narrative":"The Minor 7th scale — a major scale with lowered 3rd and 7th — is the prescribed scale for minor 7th chords: 'The Minor 7th scale is simply a Major Scale with LOWERED 3rd (b3) and LOWERED 7th (b7) tones.' Chapter 4, p. 66.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","scale-chord-compatibility"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.66"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"min7","function_role":"root-based-internalization","narrative":"Do not think of the minor 7th scale as a relative major scale starting a whole step lower: 'You will probably notice that each m7 scale has the same notes as a major scale whose root is a whole step lower. But, as cautioned before on dom. 7 scales, for your own good, don't think of the m7 scale in this way now.' Chapter 4, p. 69.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","root-based-thinking"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.69"}],"provenance":"extracted","polarity":"proscriptive"},{"chord_quality":"min7","function_role":"ii-V-I-context-application","narrative":"Minor 7th chord runs should be learned and practiced within the ii-V-I progression context: 'This particular series of sounds is one of the most common in jazz (it is known as \"ii-V-I\" if that means anything to you now)... and is a practical way, at this stage of the game, for you to become acquainted with m7 runs.' Chapter 4, p. 67.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.67"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"min7","function_role":"combining-scales-in-position","narrative":"Minor 7th scale runs should be combined with other scales (Major, Dominant 7th) within a single 5-6 fret fingerboard position, so the player can navigate the full ii-V-I without shifting. Chapter 4 explicitly names 'Combining Scales in One Position' as a technique for multi-chord soloing. Chapter 4, p. 60.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:fingerboard-position-system","position-stay-5-6-frets"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.60"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"scale-pairing-dominant-7th-scale","narrative":"The Dominant 7th scale — a major scale with a lowered 7th — is the prescribed scale for dominant 7th chords: 'The Dominant 7th scale is simply a Major scale with a lowered 7th tone.' Any chord built from some combination of (and only) these scale tones can take this scale. Chapter 3, p. 41.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","scale-chord-compatibility"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 3 p.41"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"root-based-internalization","narrative":"Do not treat the Dominant 7th scale as a major scale starting a 4th above: 'Don't fall for the \"oh, dom. 7th scales, they're really just major scales up a 4th-trap\" — it will only tend to make things harder later if you do.' Dominant 7th must be internalized from its own root. Chapter 3, p. 43.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","root-based-thinking"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 3 p.43"}],"provenance":"extracted","polarity":"proscriptive"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"group-1-dominant-run-selection","narrative":"For Group-1 dominants (chords without the 11th), select runs that contain the 3rd: 'for maximum synchronization of runs and chords, you could generalize and say that if a run contains the 3rd, use it over any of the group-1 dominants.' Runs with both or neither the 3rd and 11th work over either group. Chapter 4, p. 59.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","dominant-run-group-sync"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.59"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"group-2-dominant-run-selection","narrative":"For Group-2 dominants (chords that include the 11th), select runs that contain the 11th: 'if a run contains the 11th, use it over any of the group-2 dominants. And if a run contains both (or neither) the 3rd and 11th, use it over any chord in either group of chords. But watch out for ending or lingering tones.' Chapter 4, p. 59.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","dominant-run-group-sync"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.59"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"register-governs-extension-color","narrative":"The perceptual weight of b7 and 9 over dominant 7th chords is determined by register, not merely note choice: 'b7 and 9 really start to come alive in this \"higher\" register (it's still a fairly low register, but high enough so that these two tones don't sound like big, weighty bass tones, but rather, more like spicy lower mid-range notes).' Chapter 4, p. 58.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:fingerboard-position-system","register-governs-color"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.58"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"jazz-waltz-application","narrative":"Dominant 7th scale runs can be applied in 3/4 time for jazz waltz feel: 'You may find it highly stimulating for variety's sake, to make up some runs in 3/4 time... or even just using... the Dom. 7 scale.' This applies across Group-1 and Group-2 dominant contexts. Chapter 4, p. 71.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:rhythmic-articulation-system"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.71"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"scale-chord-compatibility-rule","narrative":"The scale-to-chord compatibility rule applies directly to dominant 7th chords: 'Any chord containing some combination of any of (but only) these chord tones, can take the Dominant 7th scale.' Chords that include non-scale tones fall outside this pairing. Chapter 3, p. 41.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","scale-chord-compatibility"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 3 p.41"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"combining-scales-in-one-position","narrative":"Major and Dominant 7th scales should be combined within a single position to allow seamless soloing across I to V chord changes: 'you will see examples of runs that combine the Major and Dom. 7th scales, in one position at a time... you will be able to stay in one little 5 or 6 fret area and play through the whole song.' Chapter 4, p. 60.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:fingerboard-position-system","position-stay-5-6-frets"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.60"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7","function_role":"arpeggio-string-set-flexibility","narrative":"When running dominant 7th type arpeggios, arpeggio tones need not be confined to the highest strings: 'These notes may be played on other strings too (5th & 4th strings).' This extends positional reach within the fingerboard area. Chapter 6, p. 107.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:fingerboard-position-system","arpeggio-string-flexibility"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 6 p.107"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7#11","function_role":"harmonic-family-membership-group-3","narrative":"Dominant chords built from the Overtone Dominant scale — which adds a #4 (#11) to the Dominant 7th scale — belong to Group 3 dominants: 'The Overtone Dominant scale is simply a Dominant 7th scale with a #4th tone instead of the regular 4th.' Chapter 4, p. 82.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 4 p.82"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7#11","function_role":"scale-pairing-overtone-dominant","narrative":"Group 3 dominant chords (with #11) take the Overtone Dominant scale (also called the Lydian Dominant scale): 'Because it contains the #4th (#11th), the Overtone Dominant scale is also called the LYDIAN Dominant scale.' The #11 is its single distinguishing feature from the plain Dominant 7th scale. Chapter 5, p. 83.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.83"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7#11","function_role":"not-an-altered-dominant","narrative":"Do not classify the Overtone Dominant / dom7#11 as an altered dominant chord: 'The Overtone Dominant scale is not considered to be an altered dominant scale — that #11 is not really a b5th, even though we may call it that — check the Overtone Series diagram again if you are in doubt.' The #11 reflects the overtone series, not chromatic alteration. Chapter 5, p. 94.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","overtone-dom-not-altered"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.94"}],"provenance":"extracted","polarity":"proscriptive"},{"chord_quality":"dom7#11","function_role":"upper-structure-triad-polytonality","narrative":"Over a dom7#11 chord using the Lydian Dominant scale, the three 'hippest' notes — the 9, #11, and 13 — form a major triad rooted a whole step above the chord root: 'the 9, #11 and 13 form a major triad whose root is a whole step above the root of the scale.' This is the device of POLYTONALITY, treated as a full chapter subject in Volume II. Chapter 5, p. 83.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","upper-structure-triad"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.83"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7#11","function_role":"chord-form-visualization-prerequisite","narrative":"Before attempting to play Overtone Dominant / Group 3 runs, the player must be able to visualize the Group 3 chord forms in that position: 'If you have trouble visualizing any of these runs, then please, for your own good, go back and learn the chord forms (group 4) for this position. This should straighten it out.' Chapter 5, p. 99.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","chord-form-prerequisite"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.99"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7alt","function_role":"altered-dominant-definition","narrative":"An altered dominant chord is any dominant 7th type chord containing one or more of: b9, #9, b5, or #5 (b13): 'Any Dom. 7th type chord that contains any one or more of the four altered tones (b9, #9, b5 and #5 or b13) will be considered as being part of what we call the GROUP 4 DOMINANT CHORDS.' Chapter 5, p. 94.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","altered-dominant-definition"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.94"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7alt","function_role":"scale-pairing-altered-dominant-types","narrative":"Group 4 altered dominant chords take one of three Altered Dominant scale types. All three types are presented in the same fingerboard position simultaneously: 'the three types of A.D. scales are all so similar that your brain, while noting the differences, can absorb them all in a kind of \"package deal\", one position at a time.' Chapter 5, p. 96.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","altered-dom-package-deal"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.96"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7alt","function_role":"package-deal-comparative-learning","narrative":"The three altered dominant scale types should be learned side by side in the same position to develop color sensitivity: 'because they are all juxtaposed in the same position, the subtle differences between them will be more evident to you, thereby increasing your sensitivity to these slightly different colors, and helping you to learn the sounds faster.' Chapter 5, p. 96.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","altered-dom-package-deal"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.96"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7alt","function_role":"chord-form-prerequisite-for-runs","narrative":"When runs in altered dominant positions are hard to visualize, the player must return to the Group 4 chord forms before proceeding: 'If you have trouble visualizing any of these runs, then please, for your own good, go back and learn the chord forms (group 4) for this position.' Chapter 5, p. 99.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","chord-form-prerequisite"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.99"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7b9","function_role":"harmonic-family-membership-group-4","narrative":"A dominant chord containing b9 qualifies as a Group 4 altered dominant chord: 'any dominant 7th scale with one or more of the following tones: b9, #9, b5 or #5 (b13)' defines the altered dominant family. The b9 tone is one of the four defining altered tones. Chapter 5, p. 94.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","altered-dominant-definition"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.94"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7#9","function_role":"harmonic-family-membership-group-4","narrative":"A dominant chord containing #9 qualifies as a Group 4 altered dominant chord. The #9 is one of the four altered tones: 'Any Dom. 7th type chord that contains any one or more of the four altered tones (b9, #9, b5 and #5 or b13) will be considered as being part of what we call the GROUP 4 DOMINANT CHORDS.' Chapter 5, p. 94.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","altered-dominant-definition"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.94"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7#9","function_role":"sharp9-substitution-or-addition","narrative":"In altered dominant contexts, the #9 may substitute for or be played alongside the natural 9: 'INSTEAD OF OR IN ADDITION TO THE #9.' This substitution rule applies across altered dominant exercises in Chapter 7. Chapter 7, p. 131.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","sharp9-substitution"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 7 p.131"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"aug7","function_role":"type-3-chord-substitution","narrative":"Over Type 3 altered dominant exercises, A7+ (augmented 7th) may be substituted for A7#9+ as a chord choice: 'As before, and on all Type 3 altered dominant pages coming up, you may wish to try A7+ for A7#9+.' This substitution allowance applies as a standing rule across all subsequent Type 3 pages. Chapter 6, p. 105.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","type3-chord-substitution"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 6 p.105"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"dom7b5","function_role":"harmonic-family-membership-group-4","narrative":"A dominant chord containing b5 qualifies as a Group 4 altered dominant chord. The b5 is one of the four defining altered tones listed in the altered dominant definition: 'any dominant 7th scale with one or more of the following tones: b9, #9, b5 or #5 (b13).' Chapter 5, p. 94.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","altered-dominant-definition"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 5 p.94"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"any","function_role":"chord-formula-derivation-from-major-scale","narrative":"All chord formulas — for any chord quality — are derived from the major scale: 'All chords have a certain group of tones called a formula, that is derived from the major scale.' The major scale is the universal reference from which every chord type is defined via raising or lowering scale degrees. Chapter 1, p. 9.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 1 p.9"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"any","function_role":"chord-takes-a-scale-rule","narrative":"The operational pairing concept: 'certain kind of chord \"takes\" a certain scale, what they mean is that that particular scale sounds good when played with that particular chord.' This governs all chord-scale pairings throughout the book. Chapter 1, p. 10.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:chord-scale-pairing","scale-chord-compatibility"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 1 p.10"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"any","function_role":"eighth-note-primary-rhythmic-unit","narrative":"Regardless of chord quality, the eighth note is jazz's default rhythmic unit for single-note lines: 'At medium and fast tempos, which most of the runs in this book are intended for, the normal unit of rhythm in jazz is the 8th note. Great players often create a very fluid sound by running long streams of 8th notes together in measure after measure.' Chapter 3, p. 39.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:rhythmic-articulation-system","8th-note-primary-unit"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 3 p.39"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"any","function_role":"swing-and-straight-both-required","narrative":"Every 8th-note run, over any chord quality, must be practiced in both swing feel and straight feel: 'all the 8th notes in this book should be played as jazz 8ths and straight 8ths, because both feels are necessary to today's music.' Chapter 3, p. 39.","source_principle_ids":["ted-greene:single-note-soloing-vol-1:rhythmic-articulation-system","swing-straight-both-required"],"source_work_id":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","references":[{"source":"single-note-soloing-vol-1","citation":"chapter 3 p.39"}],"provenance":"extracted"},{"chord_quality":"any","function_role":"swing-feel-definition","narrative":"Swing feel over any chord is produced by interpreting written straight 8ths as triplets with the middle note tied or missing: 'In the swing feel, each group of two 8th notes is actually played as if it were a group of three triplets, with the middle one tied or missing. The ear then only hears two notes, which it interprets as kind of funny 8th notes.'
